scope: Original candidate-area interview prompts, not a complete DSM criteria assessment or an APA instrument. Candidate labels are discussion areas, not diagnoses. No diagnostic scoring or probability.

candidates.label: ADHD
candidates.tier3: Have distractibility, disorganization, or acting before thinking repeatedly caused difficulty in everyday tasks?
candidates.tier4: Were similar difficulties already present in childhood and noticeable in more than one setting?
candidates.tier5: Do attention problems continue during times when sleep, mood, and anxiety are relatively settled?

candidates.label: Autism spectrum disorder
candidates.tier3: Have differences in social communication together with strong routines, focused interests, or sensory needs been a recurring part of your life?
candidates.tier4: Do these experiences trace back to early development, even if they became more apparent as demands increased?
candidates.tier5: Have social and sensory differences been present beyond periods of anxiety or isolation?

candidates.label: Specific learning disorder
candidates.tier3: Has one area such as reading, written work, or mathematics remained unusually difficult despite opportunities to learn?
candidates.tier4: Has that difficulty persisted despite targeted help, rather than occurring only when concentration or mood is worse?
candidates.tier5: Is the difficulty concentrated in a particular academic skill rather than broad learning across areas?

candidates.label: Intellectual developmental disorder / communication or motor-development concerns
candidates.tier3: Have learning, communication, movement, or everyday independence required sustained extra support since development?
candidates.tier4: Are developmental assessments or school records available to clarify which abilities and support needs are involved?
candidates.tier5: Have practical daily skills and communication been assessed alongside formal learning abilities?

candidates.label: Schizophrenia spectrum disorders
candidates.tier3: Have unusual perceptions, strongly held experiences others do not share, or disorganized thinking occurred outside sleep transitions?
candidates.tier4: Have these experiences continued outside major mood changes and affected usual functioning over time?
candidates.tier5: Have reduced motivation or organization also been observed when intense unusual perceptions or beliefs are less prominent?

candidates.label: Mood disorder with psychotic features / schizoaffective differential
candidates.tier3: Have unusual perceptions or beliefs occurred during pronounced periods of depression or unusually elevated energy?
candidates.tier4: Have unusual perceptions or beliefs also occurred when your mood and energy were close to your usual baseline?
candidates.tier5: Can you identify separate periods of mood disturbance and unusual perceptions or beliefs on a timeline?

candidates.label: Delusional disorder / circumscribed belief concerns
candidates.tier3: Has one persistent belief or closely related set of beliefs been the main concern while other thinking and daily abilities remained relatively organized?
candidates.tier4: Is the concern fairly circumscribed rather than part of broad disorganization or multiple unusual perceptions?
candidates.tier5: Do other people from your cultural or spiritual community understand the belief in a similar way?

candidates.label: Brief or evolving psychotic presentation
candidates.tier3: Did these changes begin relatively abruptly after a period of usual functioning?
candidates.tier4: Has there been a clear return toward your usual functioning, or is the course still developing?
candidates.tier5: Was the change linked to a major stressor, childbirth, sleep loss, or a medication or substance change?

candidates.label: Bipolar I disorder
candidates.tier3: Have there been distinct periods of unusually elevated or irritable energy with behavior markedly different from your usual self?
candidates.tier4: During any such period, was functioning severely disrupted, hospital care needed, or reality testing affected?
candidates.tier5: Did the high-energy change continue across settings rather than only during an exciting event or conflict?

candidates.label: Bipolar II disorder
candidates.tier3: Have noticeable periods of increased energy alternated with substantial depressive periods?
candidates.tier4: Were the higher-energy periods a clear change others noticed, even when they did not cause severe disruption?
candidates.tier5: Have there also been substantial depressive episodes and no known period of severely disruptive elevated energy?

candidates.label: Cyclothymic disorder / other bipolar-spectrum presentation
candidates.tier3: Have milder upward and downward mood shifts recurred across a long stretch of your life?
candidates.tier4: Has this fluctuating pattern been more persistent than a few isolated mood episodes?
candidates.tier5: Have more intense, clearly bounded mood episodes also occurred within the longer fluctuating pattern?

candidates.label: Major depressive disorder
candidates.tier3: Have there been distinct stretches of depressed mood or loss of interest with several other changes from your usual functioning?
candidates.tier4: Do these stretches have recognizable starts and ends rather than being your nearly constant baseline?
candidates.tier5: Have any periods of unusually increased energy or reduced need for sleep occurred separately from the low periods?

candidates.label: Persistent depressive disorder
candidates.tier3: Has a low or discouraged mood been a longstanding baseline rather than only a recent episode?
candidates.tier4: Have there been relatively few sustained periods of feeling back to your usual well baseline?
candidates.tier5: Were sustained low-mood patterns already present before the most recent worsening?

candidates.label: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder
candidates.tier3: If relevant, do marked mood symptoms repeatedly track the time before menstrual periods?
candidates.tier4: Do symptoms ease after the period begins, with a comparatively better interval in the cycle?
candidates.tier5: Have daily observations across more than one cycle confirmed the timing rather than relying on memory alone?

candidates.label: Adjustment-related depressive presentation
candidates.tier3: Did depressed mood begin in connection with a recognizable life stress or change?
candidates.tier4: Does the mood pattern closely follow that stress and its consequences rather than occurring independently?
candidates.tier5: Has the depressive pattern also occurred when the major stressor and its consequences were absent?

candidates.label: Generalized anxiety disorder
candidates.tier3: Does hard-to-control worry move across several everyday topics rather than one main trigger?
candidates.tier4: Does this broad worry persist even when a particular feared event has passed?
candidates.tier5: Is the worry broad even when there is no trauma reminder, intrusive ritual-related thought, or specific social threat?

candidates.label: Panic disorder
candidates.tier3: Have sudden surges of fear occurred unexpectedly, rather than only in a predictable feared situation?
candidates.tier4: Afterward, have you worried about another surge or changed your activities because of it?
candidates.tier5: Have medical causes or substance effects for the sudden physical surges been evaluated?

candidates.label: Social anxiety disorder
candidates.tier3: Is the central fear being judged, embarrassed, or rejected in social or performance situations?
candidates.tier4: Would the situation be substantially easier if being observed or evaluated were removed?
candidates.tier5: Is fear of negative judgment central even when leaving the situation or obtaining help would be easy?

candidates.label: Specific phobia / agoraphobia
candidates.tier3: Does fear focus on a specific object or situation, or on places where leaving or obtaining help feels difficult?
candidates.tier4: Is avoidance tied mainly to that trigger or to difficulty escaping, rather than to social evaluation?
candidates.tier5: Can you distinguish fear of the object itself from fear of panic, embarrassment, or being unable to leave?

candidates.label: Separation anxiety disorder
candidates.tier3: Is being away from an important attachment figure a main source of anxiety?
candidates.tier4: Does that concern drive repeated avoidance or difficulty functioning apart from that person?
candidates.tier5: Does the separation fear exceed concerns explained by current danger, caregiving needs, or actual instability?

candidates.label: Obsessive-compulsive disorder
candidates.tier3: Do unwanted recurring thoughts or urges lead you to repeat actions or mental rituals for relief?
candidates.tier4: Are these repetitions driven by reducing distress or preventing a feared outcome rather than by enjoyment?
candidates.tier5: Are the thoughts unwanted and intrusive, rather than beliefs you accept as accurate or ordinary everyday worries?

candidates.label: Body dysmorphic disorder
candidates.tier3: Does concern about a perceived appearance flaw lead to repeated checking, comparison, concealment, or reassurance seeking?
candidates.tier4: Is the main concern a perceived flaw beyond concerns limited to body weight or eating?
candidates.tier5: Have appearance concerns affected activities without being explained mainly by eating or weight concerns?

candidates.label: Hoarding disorder
candidates.tier3: Is letting go of possessions very distressing, allowing clutter to interfere with the use of living spaces?
candidates.tier4: Is difficulty discarding central, rather than clutter being mainly due to low energy, physical limits, or lack of resources?
candidates.tier5: Has clutter created difficulty using spaces for their intended purpose, rather than simply reflecting a collecting interest?

candidates.label: Trichotillomania / excoriation disorder
candidates.tier3: Do repeated hair pulling or skin picking cause visible effects or distress?
candidates.tier4: Have you repeatedly tried to reduce the behavior, with difficulty stopping it?
candidates.tier5: Does the pulling or picking occur outside a dermatologic problem or a deliberate effort to injure yourself?

candidates.label: Posttraumatic stress disorder
candidates.tier3: Following a frightening or harmful experience, have unwanted reminders, avoidance, and changes in mood or alertness occurred together?
candidates.tier4: Have these changes persisted beyond the immediate aftermath and remained linked to reminders of the experience?
candidates.tier5: Are the unwanted experiences linked to an event rather than primarily to generalized worry or a mood episode?

candidates.label: Acute stress presentation
candidates.tier3: Have distressing trauma-related changes begun in the recent aftermath of a frightening or harmful experience?
candidates.tier4: Is the pattern still in its early course, with its longer-term persistence not yet known?
candidates.tier5: Can the event date and the dates of symptom onset and persistence be clarified?

candidates.label: Adjustment disorder
candidates.tier3: Have emotional or behavioral difficulties followed a major stressor or life transition?
candidates.tier4: Is the stress-linked reaction a closer description than reliving a traumatic event?
candidates.tier5: Would another longstanding or independent condition better explain some of the difficulties?

candidates.label: Prolonged grief disorder
candidates.tier3: After a death, has persistent longing or preoccupation with the person been central to your difficulty?
candidates.tier4: Has grief remained deeply disruptive beyond what you and your cultural or community context would expect?
candidates.tier5: Can the clinician consider time since the loss, cultural expectations, and whether trauma or depression is also present?

candidates.label: Depersonalization/derealization disorder
candidates.tier3: Have you repeatedly felt detached from yourself or as if surroundings were unreal?
candidates.tier4: During these experiences, did you still recognize that the feeling of unreality was an experience rather than literal reality?
candidates.tier5: Do these experiences occur when fully awake and outside intoxication, migraine, or seizure-like events?

candidates.label: Dissociative amnesia
candidates.tier3: Are there gaps for important personal experiences that seem different from ordinary forgetting?
candidates.tier4: Are these gaps especially linked to stressful experiences rather than a general decline in everyday memory?
candidates.tier5: Have head injury, seizures, sleep-related events, or substance effects been considered for the memory gaps?

candidates.label: Dissociative identity presentation
candidates.tier3: Have substantial shifts in your sense of self occurred along with gaps in recall for everyday actions?
candidates.tier4: Have others described actions or conversations you cannot recall, outside ordinary forgetfulness or intoxication?
candidates.tier5: Are the shifts and memory gaps involuntary and disruptive, rather than an accepted cultural or spiritual practice?

candidates.label: Somatic symptom disorder
candidates.tier3: Do physical symptoms come with persistent health-related distress, attention, or behavior that disrupts daily life?
candidates.tier4: Does the distress remain a major difficulty even while medical evaluation or treatment is taking place?
candidates.tier5: Can you distinguish distress about physical symptoms from distress mainly about having an undetected illness?

candidates.label: Illness anxiety disorder
candidates.tier3: Is fear of having a serious illness a main problem even when physical symptoms are limited?
candidates.tier4: Does health fear persist through reassurance, repeated checking, or avoidance of medical information?
candidates.tier5: Is the central problem fear of illness rather than the physical symptoms themselves?

candidates.label: Functional neurological symptom disorder
candidates.tier3: Have movement, sensory, or seizure-like symptoms been identified for neurological assessment?
candidates.tier4: Has a qualified clinician evaluated these symptoms and discussed a functional explanation with you?
candidates.tier5: Has the evaluating clinician explained the examination findings, rather than concluding this only because tests were normal?

candidates.label: Anorexia nervosa
candidates.tier3: Have restriction and fear of weight gain or difficulty recognizing nutritional risk been central concerns?
candidates.tier4: Have these concerns continued despite significant weight loss or a clinician raising concern about low weight or malnutrition?
candidates.tier5: Have eating and weight patterns been reviewed medically alongside your own account of body image and nutritional needs?

candidates.label: Bulimia nervosa
candidates.tier3: Have episodes of feeling unable to stop eating been followed by attempts to compensate such as vomiting, fasting, or excessive exercise?
candidates.tier4: Do loss-of-control eating and compensatory actions form a recurring connected cycle?
candidates.tier5: Does the compensatory cycle occur outside periods of significantly low weight or marked restriction?

candidates.label: Binge-eating disorder
candidates.tier3: Have episodes of eating with a sense of lost control caused distress?
candidates.tier4: Do these episodes generally occur without a recurring pattern of compensatory behavior afterward?
candidates.tier5: Is lost control a central feature, rather than simply eating more than planned without distress?

candidates.label: Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder
candidates.tier3: Has eating been restricted because of sensory reactions, low interest, or fear of consequences such as choking?
candidates.tier4: Is that restriction mainly unrelated to wanting to change body shape or weight?
candidates.tier5: Have limited food access, cultural eating practices, gastrointestinal illness, and body-image concerns been considered?

candidates.label: Pica / rumination disorder
candidates.tier3: Have repeated eating of nonfood substances or returning food to the mouth been concerns?
candidates.tier4: Has the behavior occurred outside an expected developmental or cultural practice and been discussed medically?
candidates.tier5: Can the clinician clarify which behavior occurs, its frequency, and whether gastrointestinal or nutritional evaluation is needed?

candidates.label: Enuresis
candidates.tier3: Have repeated episodes of unintended urine release been a concern?
candidates.tier4: Does the pattern occur during sleep, waking hours, or both, and has a medical cause been assessed?
candidates.tier5: Did the problem follow an established period of continence, and is its onset or recurrence medically unexplained?

candidates.label: Encopresis
candidates.tier3: Have repeated bowel accidents or soiling been a concern?
candidates.tier4: Has constipation, overflow, medication effect, or another medical explanation been assessed?
candidates.tier5: Did the pattern begin after prior bowel control, and is constipation or overflow still a possible contributor?

candidates.label: Insomnia disorder
candidates.tier3: Is difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking too early a recurring concern?
candidates.tier4: Does this occur even when you have adequate opportunity and circumstances for sleep?
candidates.tier5: Do daytime effects persist after accounting for restricted sleep opportunity or an irregular schedule?

candidates.label: Hypersomnolence / narcolepsy
candidates.tier3: Is excessive sleepiness or unexpected falling asleep a recurring problem despite time available for sleep?
candidates.tier4: Have irresistible sleep episodes, unusual loss of muscle strength, or other sleep-wake events prompted specialist assessment?
candidates.tier5: Does daytime sleepiness remain after adequate sleep and after possible sleep-related breathing problems are considered?

candidates.label: Sleep-related breathing disorder
candidates.tier3: Have loud snoring, pauses in breathing, or gasping during sleep been noticed?
candidates.tier4: Has a sleep study or medical assessment been obtained for breathing during sleep?
candidates.tier5: Does the breathing concern occur independently of general worry about sleep, with observations from a sleep partner or study?

candidates.label: Circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder
candidates.tier3: Does your natural sleep timing regularly conflict with the timing required by work or daily life?
candidates.tier4: Is sleep substantially easier or more restorative when you can follow your preferred schedule?
candidates.tier5: Do symptoms track work shifts, travel, or a delayed or advanced sleep schedule?

candidates.label: Parasomnia / restless legs presentation
candidates.tier3: Have distressing dreams, unusual sleep behaviors, or an urge to move the legs disrupted sleep?
candidates.tier4: Is the main problem a recognizable event or physical sensation around sleep rather than difficulty sleeping in general?
candidates.tier5: Can the clinician distinguish dream recall, confused awakenings, dream enactment, and waking leg discomfort?

candidates.label: Sexual interest/arousal concerns
candidates.tier3: Has an unwanted change in sexual interest or arousal caused personal distress?
candidates.tier4: Is this concern present in circumstances you otherwise experience as safe, wanted, and comfortable?
candidates.tier5: Did the concern begin before or after changes in medications, hormones, health, relationships, or safety?

candidates.label: Orgasmic / ejaculation concerns
candidates.tier3: Has an unwanted change in orgasm or ejaculation caused personal distress?
candidates.tier4: Is the pattern longstanding, newly acquired, or limited to certain situations or partners?
candidates.tier5: Does the concern differ between solitary and partnered activity, without pressure to engage in unwanted activity?

candidates.label: Genito-pelvic pain/penetration concerns
candidates.tier3: Has pain, fear of pain, or difficulty with penetration been a distressing concern?
candidates.tier4: Has a medical assessment addressed pain or other physical contributors without assuming the cause is psychological?
candidates.tier5: Does pain occur in other circumstances, and has a pelvic or other relevant physical assessment been offered?

candidates.label: Gender dysphoria evaluation
candidates.tier3: Has a mismatch between experienced gender and aspects of the body or assigned gender caused personal distress?
candidates.tier4: Does the distress concern that mismatch, rather than gender diversity itself being viewed as a problem?
candidates.tier5: Can personal goals for care be clarified without assuming that any particular identity or medical treatment is required?

candidates.label: Minority stress / support needs
candidates.tier3: Have rejection, discrimination, safety concerns, or lack of support related to gender been a main source of distress?
candidates.tier4: Would improving acceptance, safety, or access to support address an important part of the distress?
candidates.tier5: Can distress from social conditions be distinguished from distress related to the body, while allowing both to coexist?

candidates.label: Intermittent explosive disorder
candidates.tier3: Have impulsive anger outbursts been much stronger than the immediate situation called for?
candidates.tier4: Are the outbursts reactive rather than planned to obtain something or intimidate someone?
candidates.tier5: Do the outbursts also occur outside intoxication, trauma reminders, or distinct high-energy mood episodes?

candidates.label: Conduct / oppositional history
candidates.tier3: Have recurring serious rule violations, aggression, or persistent conflict with authority been part of your developmental history?
candidates.tier4: Was this pattern already present before adulthood, rather than beginning only recently?
candidates.tier5: Can school, family, or other developmental accounts clarify when the behavior began and the settings involved?

candidates.label: Kleptomania / pyromania differential
candidates.tier3: Have repeated urges to steal unneeded items or set fires been followed by a sense of tension release?
candidates.tier4: Were these actions driven by the urge itself rather than money, revenge, coercion, or another goal?
candidates.tier5: Can a specialist distinguish an urge-related pattern from substance effects, elevated mood, or deliberate goal-directed behavior?

candidates.label: Substance use disorder
candidates.tier3: Has use of alcohol, drugs, or medications become hard to control or continued despite unwanted consequences?
candidates.tier4: Have attempts to cut down, obligations, relationships, or health repeatedly been affected by the pattern?
candidates.tier5: Can each substance or medication be reviewed separately, including prescribed use, pattern of use, and consequences?

candidates.label: Intoxication / withdrawal-related presentation
candidates.tier3: Do important symptoms occur around using, reducing, or stopping a substance or medication?
candidates.tier4: Does the timing repeatedly track those changes more closely than periods of stable nonuse?
candidates.tier5: Have the symptoms also occurred during a sustained stable period without intoxication, withdrawal, or medication changes?

candidates.label: Gambling disorder
candidates.tier3: Has gambling become difficult to control and continued despite financial or personal harm?
candidates.tier4: Have chasing losses, concealment, or repeated unsuccessful efforts to stop become part of the pattern?
candidates.tier5: Does gambling become problematic outside periods of unusually elevated mood or medication-related impulsivity?

candidates.label: Delirium / acute cognitive change
candidates.tier3: Has attention, awareness, or thinking changed suddenly or fluctuated markedly over a short period?
candidates.tier4: Is this a new change from baseline that has not yet received prompt medical assessment?
candidates.tier5: Has someone who knows the person confirmed an abrupt change from their usual attention or awareness?

candidates.label: Mild / major neurocognitive disorder
candidates.tier3: Has there been a gradual decline in memory, language, reasoning, or other thinking abilities from a prior level?
candidates.tier4: Has that decline affected independent management of daily tasks, beyond needing extra effort or reminders?
candidates.tier5: Can prior abilities and current independence be compared using collateral history and objective cognitive assessment?

candidates.label: Cognitive symptoms secondary to other factors
candidates.tier3: Do thinking or memory difficulties vary closely with mood, sleep, pain, medication, or substance changes?
candidates.tier4: Does thinking improve when those associated factors improve?
candidates.tier5: Have symptoms persisted after the associated mood, sleep, pain, or medication problem improved?

candidates.label: Longstanding interpersonal / emotion-regulation pattern
candidates.tier3: Have intense relationship difficulties or emotional shifts been a repeated pattern across different parts of adult life?
candidates.tier4: Has the pattern persisted outside discrete mood episodes or a recent crisis?
candidates.tier5: Can longstanding emotion and relationship patterns be distinguished from trauma responses and discrete mood episodes?

candidates.label: Longstanding detachment / mistrust pattern
candidates.tier3: Have persistent distance from others, mistrust, or unusual interpersonal experiences limited relationships?
candidates.tier4: Does this pattern occur across settings rather than only with unsafe people or in an unsupported environment?
candidates.tier5: Can mistrust or distance be understood in the context of actual threat, discrimination, neurodevelopment, and cultural norms?

candidates.label: Longstanding inhibition / dependency / rigidity pattern
candidates.tier3: Have fear of rejection, dependence on others, or rigid control repeatedly limited your choices?
candidates.tier4: Has this been a stable pattern over time rather than only a response to current stress?
candidates.tier5: Can longstanding rigidity, inhibition, or dependency be distinguished from anxiety, compulsive rituals, and current support needs?

candidates.label: Consenting sexual-interest distress evaluation
candidates.tier3: Has a recurring sexual interest caused significant personal distress or interference that you want help understanding?
candidates.tier4: Is distress present beyond discomfort caused only by others disapproving of consensual adult interests?
candidates.tier5: Can a qualified clinician review the concern without treating consensual adult interests alone as a disorder?

candidates.label: Nonconsent / harm-related specialized evaluation
candidates.tier3: Are there sexual urges or behaviors involving lack of consent, inability to consent, or risk of harm that need professional attention?
candidates.tier4: Is there a current concern about acting in a way that could harm someone or violate consent?
candidates.tier5: Can a clinician promptly review current safety, consent, access to potential victims, and protective steps directly?

context.text: Which description best fits the timing of these concerns?
For the pattern you are describing, how long has a typical uninterrupted period lasted?
When did you first notice this pattern?
choices: Recently, after a change in health or circumstances

context.text: Have these concerns caused personal distress or interfered with everyday functioning?
Could a medical condition, injury, pain, or sleep problem be contributing?
Could medications, alcohol, other substances, or changes in their use be contributing?
Could these concerns be part of another emotional, developmental, cultural, or situational pattern already discussed?

clarification.text: Can you distinguish when each concern began and whether the patterns occurred together or separately?
Have possible medical, medication, substance, developmental, and situational explanations been reviewed with a qualified clinician?
Are prior records or observations available, with your permission, to help clarify the pattern?
